title: P&IDs and ISA symbols
goals: Read an instrument tag such as FIC-101 or LSHH-204: what it measures and what it does
Say where an instrument is from its bubble: in the field, in the control room, in a PLC or DCS
Tell process lines from electrical, pneumatic and data signals
Follow a control loop on a P&ID from the transmitter to the valve, and read a valve's fail position
summary:
A **P&ID** (piping and instrumentation diagram) shows the process plant: vessels, pumps, pipes, valves, and every instrument and control loop, with how they connect. It is not to scale and not a wiring diagram. Symbols and tags follow **ANSI/ISA-5.1** (and ISO 14617 / ISO 10628 in Europe).

**Tags**: letters then a **loop number**. The **first letter** is what is measured: **F** flow, **L** level, **P** pressure, **T** temperature, **A** analysis, **S** speed, **W** weight, **Z** position. The **following letters** say what the device does: **T** transmit, **I** indicate, **C** control, **R** record, **A** alarm, **S** switch, **V** valve, **E** element (sensor), **Y** relay or compute. **H** and **L** (and HH, LL) mark high and low. So **FIC-101** is a flow indicating controller in loop 101; **LSHH-204** a level switch high-high.

Every device in a loop shares its number: **FT-101** measures, **FIC-101** controls, **FV-101** is the valve it moves.

**Bubbles** (where it is):

- circle, **no line**: in the **field**
- circle with a **solid line**: on the main **control room** panel, where the operator can reach it
- **double line**: on a **local panel**
- **dashed line**: behind a panel, not normally reachable
- circle in a **square**: a **shared display**, a DCS or HMI screen
- **hexagon**: a computer function; **diamond in a square**: a **PLC**

**Lines**: heavy solid for **process** pipes; **dashed** for **electrical** signals; a line with **pairs of short slashes** for **pneumatic** signals; a line with **small circles** for **data links** (software or comms).

**Control valves** show their actuator, and their **fail position**: **FC** fail closed, **FO** fail open, **FL** fail last (stays put) when the air or signal is lost. That choice is a safety decision.

bench.task: Get a P&ID for a part of your site (or any you can find) and trace one control loop on it. Reading only.
check: Find a transmitter (a tag with T as its second letter) and say what it measures
Follow its signal line: what kind of line is it, and where does it go?
Find the controller with the same loop number: is it in the field, a panel or the DCS/PLC?
Find the final element (the valve or drive) and its fail position
Find any alarms or trips on the same loop (letters A, S, H, L)

cards.q: On a P&ID you see the tag TIC-305. What is it?
options: A temperature indicating controller in loop 305
A timer interlock contact on line 305
A temperature transmitter, instrument 305
Test, inspect, calibrate: job 305
cards.why: ISA tags: the first letter is the measured variable (T, temperature); the next letters are what it does (I indicate, C control); the number is the loop. A transmitter would be TT-305.

cards.title: What a P&ID is for
cards.body:
A **P&ID** (piping and instrumentation diagram) shows how a process plant fits together: the **vessels**, **pumps** and **pipes**, the **valves**, and every **instrument** and **control loop**.

It shows **what connects to what**, not where things are: it is not to scale, and it is not a wiring diagram. Cable numbers and terminals are on the **loop diagrams** and wiring drawings it leads to.

Symbols and tags follow **ANSI/ISA-5.1** (in Europe often alongside ISO 10628 and ISO 14617).
cards.more:
Think of a London Underground map: it tells you which stations connect and on which line, but not how far apart they are. A P&ID does the same for a plant.

Uses on site: tracing why a level is drifting (which valve does that controller move?), planning an isolation (which valves close off this pump?), checking a change (has the drawing been updated?).

The P&ID is the master: the loop diagram for loop 101 shows the wires; the P&ID shows what loop 101 is for.

cards.q: You need the terminal numbers for a pressure transmitter's cable. Where do you look?
options: Its loop diagram or wiring drawing
The P&ID, beside the transmitter's bubble
The plant layout drawing
The pump's data sheet
cards.why: The P&ID shows what the transmitter measures and where its signal goes, not the cables and terminals. The loop diagram (or wiring drawing) for that loop has those.

cards.title: Tags: the first letter is what is measured
cards.body:
An instrument **tag** is letters then a **loop number**: **PT-102**, **LIC-201**.

The **first letter** is the **measured** (or initiating) variable:

- **F** flow, **L** level, **P** pressure, **T** temperature
- **A** analysis (pH, O₂, conductivity), **S** speed, **W** weight, **Z** position

A letter after it can modify it: **PD** is pressure difference (differential pressure), **FQ** flow quantity (a totaliser).
cards.more:
Read tags from the left: first, what it is about; then, what it does.

P is pressure, so anything starting with P is about pressure: PT transmits it, PI shows it on a gauge, PIC controls it, PSV is a pressure safety (relief) valve.

The modifier sits straight after the first letter: PDT is a differential pressure transmitter (across a filter or an orifice plate), not a 'pressure D transmitter'.

The numbering scheme varies by site: often the first digit is the plant area (loop 2xx in area 2).

cards.q: Match each first letter with what it measures.
cards.why: The first letter of an ISA tag is always the measured or initiating variable.

cards.title: The following letters: what it does
cards.body:
After the first letter come its **functions**:

- **T** transmit, **I** indicate, **R** record, **C** control
- **E** primary element (the sensor itself: a thermocouple is TE)
- **A** alarm, **S** switch (or trip)
- **V** valve or damper, **Y** relay, compute or convert (such as an I/P converter)
- **H** high, **L** low; **HH**, **LL** high-high and low-low

So **TE** is the sensor, **TT** sends its signal, **TIC** controls with it, **TV** is the valve it moves. **LSHH** is a level switch high-high: usually a trip.
cards.more:
Build them up like words. FT: flow, transmit. FIC: flow, indicate, control: a controller with a display. FY: flow, relay/convert: often the I/P converter turning the controller's 4–20 mA into 0.2–1 bar air for the valve.

Alarms: PAH is pressure alarm high; PAL low. Switches and trips: LSL is a level switch low (a pump dry-run protection); LSHH is the high-high one that trips the inlet.

The second T in TT and the first T in TT mean different things: the first is the variable (temperature), the second the function (transmit). Position in the tag decides.

options: A level switch, high-high, in loop 204
A level sensor with a heater, 204 °C
A low-speed hydraulic hoist, number 204
A line strainer, housing 204
cards.why: L level (first letter), S switch, HH high-high. A high-high switch is usually a trip that stops a tank overfilling, independent of the normal level control.

cards.title: One loop, one number
cards.body:
Every device in a control loop shares the **loop number**:

- **FE-101**: the flow element (an orifice plate, a magnetic flowmeter's tube)
- **FT-101**: the transmitter
- **FIC-101**: the controller
- **FY-101**: the I/P converter (signal to air)
- **FV-101**: the control valve

So on the drawing, and on site, you can follow a loop from sensor to valve by its number.
cards.more:
On a P&ID, loop 101 might read like this: the pipe has FE-101 in it; FT-101 beside it sends a dashed (electrical) line to a circle-in-a-square FIC-101 (the controller on the DCS screen); from there a dashed line to FY-101 near the valve; from FY-101 a line with slashes (pneumatic) to FV-101.

Read it as a sentence: measure flow, send it, control it in the DCS, turn the output into air, move the valve.

When fault-finding, the loop number is your thread: a problem on FIC-101's screen means looking at FE, FT, FY and FV-101, and their loop diagram.

cards.q: Put loop 101 in order, from the pipe to the valve.
items: FE-101: the flow element in the pipe
cards.why: Measure, transmit, control, convert to air, act: the same number all the way.

cards.title: Bubbles: where the instrument is
cards.body:
The shape round a tag says what kind of device it is, and a line through it says where:

- **Circle**, no line: in the **field**, on the plant
- Circle, **solid line** across: on the main **control room** panel, where the operator can reach it
- Circle, **double line**: on a **local panel** near the plant
- Circle, **dashed line**: behind a panel, not normally reachable
- **Circle in a square**: a **shared display**: a DCS or HMI screen
- **Hexagon**: a **computer** function
- **Diamond in a square**: a **PLC** function
cards.more:
Picture where an operator would stand. No line: out on the plant with a torch. A solid line: in the control room, at the desk. A double line: at a local panel out on the plant. A dashed line: it exists, but behind a cabinet door.

Most modern controllers are not boxes on a panel but functions in a DCS or PLC, shown on a screen: hence the circle in a square (shared display and control).

The line style is the same idea for the square and other shapes: a circle in a square with a solid line is a DCS function the operator sees in the control room.

cards.q: Match each bubble with where the instrument is.
pairs: Control room, operator can reach it

cards.title: Lines: process and signals
cards.body:
- **Heavy solid** line: a **process** pipe (with arrows for flow direction)
- Thin solid line: an instrument's connection to the process (an impulse line)
- **Dashed** line: an **electrical** signal (4–20 mA, a switch contact)
- Line with **pairs of short slashes** across it: a **pneumatic** signal (air, typically 0.2–1 bar)
- Line with **small circles** along it: a **data link** (software, fieldbus, a network)

So from the lines alone you can tell whether a signal is wires, air or comms.
cards.more:
Older drawings show dashed lines for electrical signals with slightly different marks; newer ones (ISA-5.1 2009 on) keep the dashed line for electric and use the small circles for software and data links. Check the drawing's legend sheet: every P&ID set has one.

The pneumatic line's slashes come in pairs, like //, every so often along the line.

Why it matters on site: a dashed line from a transmitter means a cable you can test with a meter; a line with slashes means an air tube, and you test it with a gauge; small circles mean a network: the fault may be in the comms, not the field.

cards.q: Match each line with what it carries.
pairs: Line with pairs of short slashes
cards.why: ISA-5.1 line types: process, electric, pneumatic, data.

cards.title: Valves and their fail position
cards.body:
Hand valves are drawn as a **bow-tie** (two triangles point to point), with a mark for the type: plain for a **gate** valve, a dot for a **globe**, a circle for a **ball**; a **check** (non-return) valve has its own arrow-like symbol.

A **control valve** is the bow-tie with its **actuator** on top: a dome for a pneumatic diaphragm, a box with M for a motor.

Its **fail position** is written beside it:

- **FC**: fail closed
- **FO**: fail open
- **FL**: fail last (stays where it was)

That is what it does if the air or the signal is lost: a safety choice.
cards.more:
Choose the fail position by asking: if the instrument air fails, which way is safe?

Fuel gas to a burner: fail closed (FC), so a power cut does not feed gas to a cold furnace.

Cooling water to a reactor: fail open (FO), so the reactor keeps cooling if control is lost.

A spring in the actuator usually does the work: air pushes against the spring, and with no air the spring drives the valve to its fail position. On the drawing you may see an arrow on the stem instead of the letters: pointing down (closing) or up (opening) on loss of air.

In a PLC the fail position also tells you what 0% output means, which matters when you scale the output.

cards.q: A control valve on the fuel gas line to a furnace is marked FC. What happens if the instrument air fails?
options: It closes, cutting the gas
It opens fully, to relieve pressure
It stays where it was
It moves to half open
cards.why: FC is fail closed: the actuator's spring shuts the valve when the air (or signal) is lost. For fuel gas that is the safe way: no gas with no control.

cards.front: What is FY-101 usually, in a flow loop with a pneumatic control valve?
cards.back: The I/P converter: it turns the controller's 4–20 mA output into the 0.2–1 bar air signal that moves FV-101.
A pressure difference (differential pressure) transmitter: across a filter, an orifice plate, or for level in a tank.

cards.q: Match each tag with what it is.
cards.why: First letter the variable (with a modifier such as Q, quantity), then the functions.

cards.q: LIC-201 is drawn as a circle inside a square, with a solid line across. Where is it?
options: A controller on the DCS or HMI screen in the control room
A level gauge mounted on the tank in the field
A switch on a local panel near the tank
A spare instrument not yet installed
cards.why: A circle in a square is a shared display and control function (DCS or HMI). The solid line says it is in the primary location, the control room, where the operator can use it.

cards.q: The line from FY-101 to FV-101 has pairs of short slashes across it. What does that tell you to test it with?
options: A pressure gauge: it is an air signal
A multimeter: it is a 4–20 mA signal
A network tester: it is a fieldbus
Nothing: it is a process pipe
cards.why: Slashes in pairs mark a pneumatic signal: typically 0.2 to 1 bar from the I/P converter to the valve actuator.

cards.q: Why might the cooling-water valve on a reactor be FO (fail open)?
options: So cooling continues if control is lost
Because FO valves are cheaper to buy
So the reactor cools more slowly on a trip
All control valves must be fail open
cards.why: If air or signal fails, the safe state for a reactor is full cooling. Each valve's fail position is chosen for that valve's process: fuel gas usually FC, cooling usually FO.

cards.q: Which of these is in the same loop as PIC-310?
options: TIC-310's valve TV-301
PIC-311
cards.why: Devices in one loop share the loop number. PT-310 is the pressure transmitter feeding PIC-310.

options: A level transmitter in loop 115
A limit timer set to 115 s
A low-temperature alarm, number 115
A level trip set at 115%

cards.q: Match each tag with what it is.
Match each line with its signal.
Match each mark with what the valve does on loss of air.
